summary: Describes a periodic sampling method and metrics for assessing IP network performance, and argues for it as an alternative to the Poisson sampling in RFC 2330. Periodic streams suit measuring traffic that resembles constant bit rate flows such as voice, and apply to both active and passive measurements.

plainLanguage.summary: This document measures the network the way a video call uses it: by sending packets of the same size at even intervals and timing each one. The starting point is chosen at random so that the test cannot be anticipated, and the results cover delay, delay variation and loss.

questions: what is a periodic stream in network measurement
how to measure one way delay
why use periodic sampling instead of poisson
subtitle: Send packets at steady, evenly spaced times to measure the delay and loss that real-time media would see.

tldr.problem: A sample of network measurements taken at random times only covers part of the performance spectrum, and it does not resemble the traffic an interactive application actually sends.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a sampling method that sends equally sized packets at a fixed interval between a randomly chosen start time and a stop time, together with the metric Type-P-One-way-Delay-Periodic-Stream and the delay, delay variation and loss figures derived from it.
tldr.outcome: The method works for active and passive measurement, simulates constant bit rate traffic such as voice, and simplifies some analysis, while random start times and finite-length tests keep the samples from being predictable.

today: RFC 3432 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a companion to the framework in RFC 2330 and to the one-way delay metric in RFC 2679, and it defines no protocol and no well-known values, so it has no IANA actions.

sections.title: Why Periodic Sampling
sections.content:
The original driver for this work was quality of service for interactive periodic streams, such as multimedia conferencing over IP, but the idea of periodic sampling and measurement has wider applicability. Transmitting equally sized packets, or mostly same-size packets, through a network at regular intervals simulates a constant bit-rate, or nearly constant bit-rate, multimedia bit stream; these packets are called periodic streams. Cases of mostly same-size packets may be found in applications that have multiple coding methods, for example digitally coded comfort noise during silence gaps in speech.

The IPPM framework notes that a sample metric using regularly spaced singleton tests has some limitations from a general measurement point of view: only part of the network performance spectrum is sampled. Some applications also sample this limited performance spectrum, and their performance may be of critical interest.

Periodic sampling is useful for four stated reasons. It is applicable to passive measurement as well as active measurement. An active measurement can be configured to match the characteristics of media flows, which simplifies the estimation of application performance. Measurements of many network impairments, such as delay variation, consecutive loss and reordering, are sensitive to the sampling frequency, and when the impairments themselves are time-varying, with the variations somewhat rare yet important, a constant sampling frequency simplifies analysis. And frequency domain analysis is simplified when the samples are equally spaced.

Simulation of constant bit rate flows with periodic streams encourages dense sampling of network performance, since typical multimedia flows have 10 to 100 packets in each second. Dense sampling permits the characterization of network phenomena with short duration.
sections.plainLanguage: Regularly spaced tests only cover part of what a network does, but the part they cover is the part that matters for a voice or video call. Sending packets at a steady rate also imitates the real traffic closely, which makes the numbers easier to trust.

sections.title: The Sampling Methodology
sections.content:
The Framework points out two potential problems with periodic sampling. The performance sampled may be synchronized with some other periodic behavior, or the samples may be anticipated and the results manipulated; unpredictable sampling is preferred. And active measurements can cause congestion, and periodic sampling might drive congestion-aware senders into a synchronized state, producing atypical results.

Poisson sampling produces an unbiased sample for the various IP performance metrics, yet there are situations where alternative sampling methods are advantageous. The document prescribes periodic sampling methods that address the problems above. Predictability and some forms of synchronization can be mitigated through the use of random start times and limited stream duration over a test interval. The periodic sampling parameters produce bias, and judicious selection can produce a known bias of interest. The total traffic generated by this or any sampling method should be limited to avoid adverse effects on non-test traffic, so packet size, packet rate, and sample duration and frequency should all be considered.

The configuration parameters of periodic sampling are five. T is the beginning of a time interval where a periodic sample is desired. dT is the duration of the interval for allowed sample start times. T0 is a time that MUST be selected at random from the interval [T, T+dT] to start generating packets and taking measurements. Tf is a time, greater than T0, for stopping the generation of packets for a sample, and it may be relative to T0 if desired. incT is the nominal duration of the inter-packet interval, first bit to first bit.

T0 may be drawn from a uniform distribution, that is T0 = T + Unif(0,dT), and other distributions may also be appropriate. Start times in successive time intervals MUST use an independent value drawn from the distribution. In passive measurement, the arrival of user media flows may have sufficient randomness, or a randomized start time of the measurement during a flow may be needed to meet this requirement. When a mix of packet sizes is desired, passive measurements usually possess the sequence and statistics of sizes in actual use, while active measurements would need to reproduce the intended distribution of sizes.
sections.plainLanguage: Five numbers define a test: when it may start, how long the start time may be spread out, the start time itself, when to stop, and how far apart the packets go. The start time is picked at random each time, so a repeated test never runs at the same moment twice.

sections.title: The Metric and Its Parameters
sections.content:
The sample metric presented here is similar to the sample metric Type-P-One-way-Delay-Poisson-Stream in RFC 2679, and the singletons defined in the Framework and in that document are applicable here. The metric is named Type-P-One-way-Delay-Periodic-Stream.

The global metric parameters apply in all the sub-sections. Each singleton usually includes Src, the IP address of a host; Dst, the IP address of a host; IPV, the IP version used in the measurement; dTloss, a time interval that is the maximum waiting time for a packet before declaring it lost; and packet size p(j), the desired number of bytes in the Type-P packet, where j is the size index. The optional parameters are PktType, any additional qualifiers such as a transport address, and Tcons, a time interval for consolidating parameters collected at the measurement points. While a number of applications will use one packet size, with j = 1, other applications may use packets of different sizes. Especially in cases of congestion, it may be useful to use packets smaller than the maximum or predominant size of packets in the periodic stream. A topology where Src and Dst are separate from the measurement points is assumed.

At the source measurement point MP(Src), each singleton usually includes Tstamp(Src)[i], the time of packet i as measured there. The additional parameters are PktID(Src)[i], a unique identification or sequence number for each packet, and PktSi(Src)[i], the actual packet size. At the destination measurement point MP(Dst), the same three quantities are collected: Tstamp(Dst)[i], PktID(Dst)[i] and PktSi(Dst)[i]. The optional parameters there are dTstop, a time interval added to Tf to determine when to stop collecting metrics for a sample, and PktStatus[i], the status of each packet received, where possible status includes OK, packet header corrupt, packet payload corrupt, duplicate and fragment. The criteria to determine the status MUST be specified if used.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet is stamped with a time at the sending side and again at the receiving side, and given an identifier so the two stamps can be matched up. The receiver also notes what was wrong with each packet, if anything.

sections.title: Computing Delay, Delay Variation and Loss
sections.content:
Using the parameters above, a delay singleton is calculated as Delay[i] = Tstamp(Dst)[i] - Tstamp(Src)[i], for each packet i.

For several conditions it will not be possible to compute delay singletons. If a packet is spurious, there is no Tstamp(Src)[i] time. If it is not received, there is no Tstamp(Dst)[i]. If the packet header is corrupt, there is no Tstamp(Dst)[i]. If it is a duplicate, only the first non-corrupt copy of the packet received at the destination should have Delay[i] computed.

A sample metric for average delay is AveDelay = (1/N) times the sum of Delay[i] from i = 1 to N, assuming all packets from 1 through N have valid singletons.

A delay variation singleton can also be computed. IPDV[i], for each packet i except the first one, is the delay variation between successive packets, calculated as IPDV[i] = Delay[i] - Delay[i-1]. IPDV[i] may be negative, zero or positive, and the delay singletons for packets i and i-1 must be calculable or IPDV[i] is undefined. An example metric for the IPDV sample is the range, RangeIPDV = max(IPDV[]) - min(IPDV[]).

The procedure for collecting a sample runs as follows. Beginning on or after time T0, Type-P packets are generated by Src and sent to Dst until time Tf is reached, with a nominal interval between the first bit of successive packets of incT as measured at MP(Src). The interval may be nominal for a number of reasons, such as variation in packet generation at Src and clock issues. MP(Src) records the parameters above only for packets with timestamps between and including T0 and Tf that have the required Src, Dst and any other qualifiers, and MP(Dst) also records for packets with timestamps between T0 and Tf plus dTstop.

Optionally at a time Tf plus Tcons, but eventually in all cases, the data from MP(Src) and MP(Dst) are consolidated to derive the sample metric results. To prevent stopping data collection too soon, dTcons should be greater than or equal to dTstop. Conversely, to keep data collection reasonably efficient, dTstop should be some reasonable time interval, even if dTloss is infinite or extremely long.
sections.plainLanguage: Subtract the sending time from the receiving time to get the delay for one packet. Subtract one packet's delay from the next to get how much the delay jumped, and the gap between the biggest and smallest of those jumps is one summary figure.

sections.title: Errors, Clocks and Calibration
sections.content:
The description of any specific measurement method should account for sources of error or uncertainty. Three are noted for periodic streams and delay metrics: error due to variation of incT, whose reasons can be uneven process scheduling, possibly due to CPU load; errors or uncertainties due to uncertainties in the clocks of the MP(Src) and MP(Dst) measurement points; and errors or uncertainties due to the difference between wire time and host time.

On clocks, any error in the synchronization between the MP(Src) clock and the MP(Dst) clock contributes to error in the delay measurement. The two clocks have a synchronization error of Tsynch if the MP(Src) clock is Tsynch ahead of the MP(Dst) clock, so if the value of Tsynch is known exactly it could be used to correct the delay. The resolution of a clock adds to uncertainty about any time measured with it, so a source clock with a resolution of 10 msec adds 10 msec of uncertainty to any time value measured with it; the resolutions are denoted ResMP(Src) and ResMP(Dst). The skew of a clock is not so much an additional issue as a realization that Tsynch is itself a function of time, so any attempt to measure or bound it must be repeated periodically. The function Esynch(t) denotes an upper bound on the uncertainty in synchronization, so |Tsynch(t)| is at most Esynch(t). Naive computation of Tstamp(Dst)[i] minus Tstamp(Src)[i] will be off by Tsynch(t) plus or minus the sum of the two resolutions, and the clock-related problems introduce a total uncertainty of Esynch(t) + Rsource + Rdest.

On wire time against host time, the metric would like to measure the time between when a packet is measured and time-stamped at MP(Src) and when it arrives and is time-stamped at MP(Dst). If timestamps are applied by software on Src and Dst, that software can only directly measure the time between when Src generates the packet and when Dst has started to process it; these are host times. Hsource is an upper bound on the uncertainty in the difference between wire time of MP(Src) and host time on the Src host, and Hdest is defined similarly for the destination, and these introduce a total uncertainty of Hsource + Hdest.

Calibration decomposes measured values as measured value equals true value plus systematic error plus random error. If the systematic error, the constant bias, can be determined it can be compensated for, leaving reported value equals true value plus random error. At a minimum, a bound should be found such that the reported value is in the range of true value minus e to true value plus e at least 95 percent of the time; e is the calibration error, and it represents the degree to which the values produced by the measurement instrument are repeatable. Adding up the individual uncertainties gives Esynch(t) + ResMP(Src) + ResMP(Dst) + Hsource + Hdest.

Reasonable bounds on both the clock-related uncertainty and the host-related uncertainty should be possible by careful design and by calibrating the instruments using a known, isolated network in a lab. The clock-related uncertainties are greatly reduced through the use of a GPS time source, since the sum of Esynch(t) plus the two resolutions is small and bounded for the duration of the measurement because of the global time source. The host-related uncertainties could be bounded by connecting two instruments back to back with a high-speed serial link or isolated LAN segment, so that repeated measurements measure the same one-way delay. If the test packets are small, such a connection has a minimal delay that may be approximated by zero, so the measured delay contains only systematic and random error in the instrumentation; the average value of repeated measurements is the systematic error and the variation is the random error. One way to compute the systematic error and the random error to a 95 percent confidence is to repeat the experiment many times, at least hundreds of tests: the systematic error would then be the median, and the random error could be found by removing it from the measured values. The 95 percent confidence interval would be the range from the 2.5th percentile to the 97.5th percentile of these deviations, and the calibration error e could be taken as the largest absolute value of these two numbers, plus the clock-related uncertainty.

Random error is a function of measurement load, so calibration measurements should be performed with the same measurement load that the instruments will see in the field, in addition to minimal load measurements to find the systematic error.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends need clocks that agree, and the software that stamps the packets adds its own delay on top. The document gives a formula that adds up all of these sources of error, and a way to measure the instrument's own error in a lab with the two ends wired together.

sections.title: What the Results Can Tell You
sections.content:
Figure 1 of the document shows measurements on multiple protocol levels, from application down to physical. The user's focus is on transport quality evaluation from the application point of view, but to properly separate the quality contribution of the operating system and the codec on packet voice, it is beneficial to be able to measure quality at the IP level. Link layer monitoring provides a way of accounting for link layer characteristics such as bit error rates.

In general, the results of measurements may be influenced by individual application requirements and responses. Applications have varying tolerance to lost packets, and the distribution of lost packets, whether random or bursty, matters. Many applications treat packets delayed longer than a certain value as equivalent to lost packets. Some applications may be perturbed by duplicate packets, and by reordering, which may be in addition to the possibility of exceeding the long delay threshold as a result of being out of sequence. Most applications will probably treat a packet with a corrupt header as equivalent to a lost packet. Some applications, such as digital voice codecs, may accept a corrupt payload, and the payload may contain application-specific forward error correction that can compensate for some level of corruption. A destination may receive spurious packets, packets that are not sent by the source as part of the metric, and many applications may be perturbed by them. Depending on the observed protocol level, some of these issues may be indistinguishable from others by the application, but it may be important to preserve the distinction for the operators of Src, Dst and the intermediate networks.

The reference measurement setup for all measurement types has a source host, a destination host and corresponding measurement points MP(Src) and MP(Dst). Separate equipment for the measurement points may be used if having Src or Dst conduct the measurement would significantly affect the delay performance to be measured. MP(Src) should be placed close to the egress point of packets from Src, and MP(Dst) close to the ingress point of packets for Dst, close being defined as a distance sufficiently small so that application-level performance characteristics measured can be expected to follow the corresponding performance characteristic between Src and Dst to an adequate accuracy. The basic principle is that results between MP(Src) and MP(Dst) should be the same as for a measurement between Src and Dst, within the general error margin target of the measurement, for example under 1 ms, with the number of lost packets the same.

Three forms of measurement are described. One-way measurement only yields information on network behaviour in one direction, and the stream at the network transport level does not emulate accurately a full-duplex multimedia connection. Paired one-way delay refers to two multimedia streams, Src to Dst and Dst to Src, for the same Src and Dst; for some applications the delay performance of each one-way path matters more than the round-trip delay, as for delay-limited signals such as VoIP. The example given shows Src to Dst with an average delay of 30 ms and Dst to Src with an average delay of 120 ms, which to a round-trip measurement would look like an average of 150 ms delay; without the knowledge of the asymmetry, a problem that the application at either end may have with delays averaging more than 100 ms might be missed. Round-trip measurement has two advantages from the point of view of periodic multimedia streams: it avoids the need of host clock synchronization, and it allows for a simulation of full-duplex communication. The downsides are the need for more bandwidth than a one-way test and more complex accounting of packet loss. The returning stream may be more bursty than the one on the first leg of the round-trip journey, so the performance estimates obtained are pessimistic, and the possibility of asymmetric routing and queuing must be taken into account during an analysis of the results.
sections.plainLanguage: You can measure in one direction, in both directions at once, or as a round trip. Measuring both directions separately is what shows up an asymmetric path, where the way back is much slower than the way out, which a round-trip number would hide.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This method generates a periodic stream of packets from one host to another through intervening networks, and it could be abused for denial of service attacks directed at the destination and the intervening networks. Administrators of the source, the destination and the intervening networks should establish bilateral or multi-lateral agreements regarding the timing, size and frequency of collection of sample metrics. Use of the method in excess of the terms agreed between the participants may be cause for immediate rejection, discard of packets, or other escalation procedures defined between the affected parties.

Active use of this method generates packets for a sample rather than taking samples based on user data, and does not threaten user data confidentiality. Passive measurement must restrict attention to the headers of interest. Since user payloads may be temporarily stored for length analysis, suitable precautions MUST be taken to keep this information safe and confidential.

It may be possible to identify that a certain packet or stream of packets is part of a sample. With that knowledge at the destination or in the intervening networks, it is possible to change the processing of the packets, for example increasing or decreasing delay, in a way that distorts the measured performance. It may also be possible to generate additional packets that appear to be part of the sample metric, which are likely to perturb the results. To discourage this, packet interference checks such as a cryptographic hash MAY be used.
sections.plainLanguage: A steady stream of test packets is a load on the network, so the operators should agree on how much of it is acceptable. And if the test packets look recognisable, someone could treat them specially and make the numbers wrong.

messages.note: Recorded for packets between T0 and Tf.

messages.label: Tstamp(Dst)[i]
messages.note: Recorded for packets between T0 and Tf plus dTstop.

viz.caption: THE DELAY AND DELAY VARIATION FORMULAS (SECTION 4.2.4)

data.title: Derived metrics
data.code:
Delay[i] = Tstamp(Dst)[i] - Tstamp(Src)[i]

AveDelay = (1/N) Sum(from i=1 to N, Delay[i])

IPDV[i] = Delay[i] - Delay[i-1]

RangeIPDV = max(IPDV[]) - min(IPDV[])

viz.caption: THREE WAYS TO MEASURE A STREAM

cells: Only covers one direction, so it does not emulate a full-duplex connection.
Two streams, Src to Dst and Dst to Src.
More traffic, but it exposes asymmetric paths that a round-trip number hides.
More bandwidth than a one-way test, more complex loss accounting, and pessimistic estimates if the return stream is burstier.

items.title: Esynch(t)
items.text: An upper bound on the uncertainty in synchronizing the two measurement point clocks.

items.title: ResMP(Src)
items.text: The resolution of the source measurement point clock; a 10 msec resolution adds 10 msec of uncertainty.

items.title: ResMP(Dst)
items.text: The resolution of the destination measurement point clock.

items.title: Hsource
items.text: Uncertainty in the gap between wire time and host time at the source.

items.title: Hdest
items.text: Uncertainty in the gap between host time and wire time at the destination.
